blocks.en: Hello, young explorers, and welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
This is our eighteenth show together!
Today, two hot mysteries.
First, the hottest pepper ever — so hot that only five people have ever eaten a whole one.
Then, a kitchen puzzle: can hot water turn into ice faster than cold water?
Let's go!
Meet Pepper X, the hottest chilli pepper of all.
It grows in South Carolina, in America, under green leaves.
Its grower is Ed Currie, a pepper scientist with a dream.
He mixed pepper plants again and again — and after ten years, Pepper X was born.
How hot is it?
Scientists measure pepper heat with the Scoville scale.
A jalapeño pepper reads about five thousand.
Pepper X?
The lab reading astonished everyone: nearly two million, seven hundred thousand!
That is more than five hundred times hotter than a jalapeño.
Guinness gave Pepper X the crown: hottest pepper ever measured.
Why is Pepper X so hot?
The fire lives in capsaicin, a chemical in the white skin that holds the seeds.
Pepper X is small and wrinkly, and the wrinkles give that skin more room to grow, so it makes much more fire.
Only five people have eaten a whole one.
They sweat, cry, and the media film it.
Do not worry — the fire is a trick.
Capsaicin shouts “Fire!” to your nerves, but it cannot really burn or damage you.
Water cannot wash it away.
Milk can — milk carries fat.
Now fly to Tanzania, in Africa, to meet a schoolboy, Erasto Mpemba.
His class made ice cream from boiled milk and sugar.
One day, with the freezer nearly full, Mpemba pushed his hot mix straight in — no waiting for it to cool.
Later, Mpemba checked the freezer — and stared.
His hot mix was ice cream, but his classmate's cold mix was still soft!
He asked his teacher why, but the teacher just laughed: “Mpemba's physics!” The whole class erupted in laughter.
The question stayed in his head.
Years later, a scientist, Dr Denis Osborne, visited Mpemba's new school.

He asked again: “Two cups of water, one at thirty-five degrees and one at one hundred — why does the hotter one freeze first?” Osborne returned to his laboratory, tested the idea again, and was astonished: the student was right.
They published the answer together, and the effect now carries Mpemba's name.
So why can hot water win the race to ice?
Scientists still argue about the answer.
Hot water steams, so some of it flies away — less water is left to freeze.
It also swims in slow circles, carrying heat out faster.
But it does not always work.
It needs the right cups, the right temperatures — the right conditions.
Then hot really can beat cold!
Here's today's idiom: “in hot water.” But nobody is cooking, and nobody is taking a bath!
If you are in hot water, you are in trouble.
Here's an example: “Tom forgot his homework again, so now he is in hot water with his teacher.” Poor Mpemba asked about hot water — he was never in it!
Let's think about our stories.
Two questions.
First: if you could grow a record-breaking food in your garden, what would it be — the biggest, the sweetest, or the hottest?
Second: Mpemba believed his own eyes, even when everyone laughed.
What strange thing have you noticed that nobody believed?
Talk about it with your family!
That's all for today, young explorers.
Stay curious, ask brave questions — and keep out of hot water!
See you tomorrow morning!
